rows.description: A teenager delays a project because a poor result would reveal weakness; putting it off protects the self-image but makes the eventual work worse.

A teenager tells themself they work better under pressure, or that they will start after one video. Excuses feel reasonable in the moment, and the delay is really about avoiding an unpleasant feeling, not about time.

rows.subtype: Feeling like a fraud in a top college [Actor]
rows.description: A student admitted to a prestigious institute believes they got in by luck and that everyone will soon find out; success is discounted while comparison with others is harsh.

rows.subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
rows.description: A manager gives specific, honest praise to a newcomer who doubts themself, naming what was done well. Vague praise is discounted, and concrete feedback offers something the doubting mind can accept.

rows.subtype: Restless and asking what to do [Actor]
rows.description: A child declares boredom after ten minutes and wants a screen; boredom is uncomfortable but can also be the doorway to imagination when adults give time and simple materials.
A child grasps ideas far above age level yet still needs friends, play and comfort. Boredom, perfectionism and feeling different are common, and adults must nurture the whole child, not only marks.

rows.subtype: Friend all good then all bad [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager describes a friend as perfect one week and as a total traitor the next after a small slight; strong feelings make it hard to hold both good and disappointing sides together.

rows.subtype: Sharing tasks in a student group [Actor]
rows.description: A group leader in a project either takes everything or hands out pieces with no check-in, and members either resent the load or vanish. Fair splitting needs clear owners and one agreed checkpoint.

rows.subtype: Restless and asking what to do [Actor]
rows.description: A child declares boredom after ten minutes and wants a screen; boredom is uncomfortable but can also be the doorway to imagination when adults give time and simple materials.
A teenager who drags out a word such as fiiine may signal reluctance, boredom or sarcasm. The rhythm can contradict the words, so a friend or parent reads both, then asks a gentle check.
A child who takes longer with reading calls themselves dumb and stops trying; a single label replaces a specific skill that can be practised.
Grabs back, shouts or bites; learns through adult labelling ("you are angry") that feeling is allowed but hitting is not.
